newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN chief unveils welter of reforms for world body.
newsitem.headline: UN chief unveils welter of reforms for world body.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Wednesday unveiled much-anticipated plans to overhaul the U.N. bureaucracy, shrink budgets, merge programmes and put the money he saves at work in poor nations.

Calling his proposals a "quiet revolution," Annan in a 90-page report said the United Nations was becoming increasingly "fragmented, duplicative and rigid," often unable to find meet expectations with accomplishments.

For some, particularly critics in the U.S. Congress, the revolution may be too quiet. No one proposal is striking on its own, but the combination of the complicated reforms is expected to change the way the world body does business.

The U.S. Senate is moving toward appropriating $819 million of the $1.6 billion in arrears owed to the United Nations. Conditions are attached to the payment, many of which the United Nations can meet, but others are strongly opposed by the rest of the world as eccentric.

Specifically, Annan recommends the appointment of a second in command, expected to be a woman, the creation of a cabinet that would cut by a third the 27 senior officials reporting to him and the merging of several departments.

In an apparent effort to get the support of the Third World, which holds a majority in the General Assembly, Annan proposes that savings -- expected to reach $200 million in several years -- be put in a new fund for economic assistance programmes for poor nations.

The proposals create a cabinet in four groupings -- peace and security, economic and social affairs, development and humanitarian affairs -- and thereby downgrade administration and support services in major decision-making.

Human rights issues will get a higher profile both in the cabinet and under a new plan to put the Geneva-based Centre for Human Rights under Irish President Mary Robinson, who will become U.N. Higher Commissioner for Human Rights.
"There are changes in this institution both staff and governments are going to feel in the daily conduct of its work," said Shashi Tharoor, an official in Annan's office.

His new plans build on reforms announced since he took office in January -- removing 1,000 jobs from the budget, holding or reducing the budget to $1.3 billion a year, cutting administrative costs from 38 percent to 25 percent, reducing paperwork by 40 percent until the end of the year.
But there are no wholesale firings. With the average staff age at 49, half of the 9,000 employees in the secretariat or the main bureaucracy will be retiring in the next 10 years.

Some of the more radical proposals died before they even reached Annan, especially among key semi-autonomous agencies who have their own boards and fund-raising and whose combined staff more than doubles that of the main secretariat.
Private aid groups have complained for years that U.N. agencies worked at cross purposes in the same country and several of Annan's predecessors have attempted to stop it.

Carol Bellamy, the director of the U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF), used her considerable political skills as a former New York City Council president to campaign openly against any possible lost of identity for her agency, should any of its duties be transferred elsewhere.
And Catherine Bertini, the U.S. director of the World Food Programme, which is one of three Rome-based agencies dealing with agriculture, was said to oppose almost all changes.

The new plan groups UNICEF, the U.N. Population Fund and the U.N. Development Programme (UNDP) under the chairmanship of Gustave Speth, the American UNDP director for coordination purposes, without changing the structure of the agencies.
Plans also were dropped to abolish the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs, which has been unable to coordinate the stronger individual agencies.

But it is a favourite among Europeans and now will be replaced by a smaller relief coordinator's office and represent the Geneva-based U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, the World Food Programme and others in the cabinet.
"Calls for cuts were loud and clear," said Ruggie, "but not the programme I most care about."
